sections.title: Pawn structures
paras: Pawns can’t move backward, so every pawn move changes the position for good. The pawn structure decides where the pieces belong and which plans make sense.

An isolated pawn has no friendly pawns on the neighbouring files, so no pawn can ever defend it. Doubled pawns stand on the same file and can’t protect each other. A passed pawn has no enemy pawns in front of it on its own file or the neighbouring files, so only pieces can stop it.
Being able to name these features at a glance is the first step toward making plans around them.
sections.key: Isolated pawns can’t be defended by pawns, doubled pawns can’t defend each other, and passed pawns can only be stopped by pieces.

sections.title: Piece activity
paras: An active piece controls many squares and has targets to attack. A passive piece defends, blocks its own pawns or has nowhere to go. Positional play often comes down to improving your worst piece while limiting your opponent’s best one.
Open files belong to rooks, long diagonals to bishops, and central squares that pawns can’t attack to knights. When you can’t find a plan, find your least active piece and give it a better square.
In the training positions, the best move is a quiet one: no check, no capture, just a stronger placement or a move that takes something away from the opponent.
sections.key: When there is nothing to calculate, improve your worst piece.

sections.title: Weak squares and outposts
paras: A square that no enemy pawn can ever attack is a weak square for your opponent and a potential outpost for you. A knight placed on an outpost, especially one supported by a pawn, is very hard to remove: it can only be challenged by trading it for another piece.
Outposts are created by pawn moves. Once the neighbouring pawns have advanced past a square or disappeared, that square can never be covered by a pawn again.
In these exercises an outpost means a square on White’s fourth, fifth or sixth rank that no black pawn can ever attack and that a white pawn defends.
sections.key: Before placing a piece, ask: can a pawn ever drive it away? If not, the square may be worth several moves to reach.

sections.title: Good and bad pieces
paras: A bishop is bad when most of its own pawns stand on squares of its color. Those pawns block it and leave the opposite-colored squares without protection. A bishop is good when its pawns stand on the other color, leaving it free to move.
Pawn structure decides which minor pieces are worth keeping. In closed positions with fixed pawns, knights often outperform bad bishops; in open positions, bishops usually come into their own.
In these exercises, a bishop counts as bad when at least 70% of its side’s pawns stand on its color, and good when no more than 30% do.
sections.key: Count your pawns on each color. A bishop that shares a color with most of its pawns is a bad bishop.

items.question: Is Black’s bishop on g7 a good bishop or a bad bishop?
items.explanation: Of Black’s 5 pawns, 1 stand on dark squares, the same color as the bishop. Its pawns are mostly on the other color, leaving it free to move, so it is a good bishop.

items.question: Is Black’s bishop on d6 a good bishop or a bad bishop?
items.explanation: Of Black’s 5 pawns, 4 stand on dark squares, the same color as the bishop. They block it and leave the other color weak, so it is a bad bishop.

items.question: Is Black’s bishop on f6 a good bishop or a bad bishop?
items.explanation: Of Black’s 7 pawns, 5 stand on dark squares, the same color as the bishop. They block it and leave the other color weak, so it is a bad bishop.

items.question: Is Black’s bishop on g7 a good bishop or a bad bishop?
items.explanation: Of Black’s 6 pawns, 1 stand on dark squares, the same color as the bishop. Its pawns are mostly on the other color, leaving it free to move, so it is a good bishop.

sections.title: Exchanges
paras: Every exchange changes the character of the position. Trade pieces when you are ahead in material, when you are defending against an attack, or when the trade leaves your opponent with a weakness. Avoid trades when you are cramped and need your pieces, or when your opponent’s remaining piece would be much better than yours.
The question to ask before any trade is: which piece will remain, and is it better or worse than the one I am giving up?
Several of the positions that follow turn on this question.
sections.key: Before you trade, compare the pieces that will remain on the board.

sections.title: Planning in quiet positions
paras: A practical method for quiet positions: first assess the pawn structure, then list the weaknesses on both sides, then decide where to play, usually on the side of the board where your pawns point and your pieces are better placed.
A plan doesn’t need to be long. Two or three moves that improve your position and take something away from your opponent are often enough.
sections.key: Structure, weaknesses, then the side of the board to play on.

sections.title: Training exercises
paras: A mixed set that combines structural judgments with quiet best moves.
sections.key: Name the structure first; the best moves follow from it.
